# Chabbisodhana Sutta (MN 112 (PTS MN iii 29))

**ID:** MN 112 (PTS MN iii 29)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)

**Title (Pali):** Chabbisodhana Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Sixfold Purification

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Chabbisodhana Sutta* (MN 112; PTS MN iii 29) sets forth the procedure for interrogating and verifying a mendicant's claim to awakening (*arahantship*) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo, Scope of Free Inquiry; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. When a monk declares that he has attained arahantship, his claim is neither to be immediately accepted nor dismissed; instead, fellow practitioners should examine his realization with specific sets of detailed questions [SuttaCentral; Anālayo, Scope of Free Inquiry; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. Although the sutta's title announces an exposition of a "sixfold" purification, the extant Pali text details questions regarding only five topics: (1) four modes of communication or sense data (what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized); (2) the five clinging aggregates; (3) the six internal and external elements (where the arahant neither identifies an element as self nor possesses a sense of self based on it); (4) the twelve sense bases; and (5) the body with consciousness together with all external signs [Anālayo 2014; Lin 2015; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. In outlining the path to destruction of the corruptions, the discourse depicts the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) as being attained directly after the four *jhānas*, applying a fourfold analytical method to the *āsavas* (knowing them, their arising, their cessation, and the way leading to their cessation) [Anderson 1999; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka].

The numerical inconsistency between the "sixfold" title and the five topics preserved in the discourse is addressed in the Pali commentary (*Papañcasūdanī*), which records an opinion of Indian monks noting that an additional category of purification—preserved in the Chinese parallel MĀ 187—was originally part of the text, pointing to an accidental loss of material during the Pali text's transmission history [Anālayo, Dawn of Abhidharma; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. SuttaCentral records the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* discourse MĀ 187 as the primary full parallel, alongside a parallel in the Saṁyutta Nikāya (SN 35.120) and thematic parallels across numerous Nikāya discourses, while noting references to the sutta in the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 14) and *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 10.3, Kv 18.9) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus reports widespread internal Pali reuse, identifying the most extensive textual alignments with AN 4, AN 10, the *Catukkapuggalapaññatti* (Pp 2.4), DN 33 (*Saṅgīti Sutta*), and DN 2 (*Sāmaññaphala Sutta*) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus's automated cross-language alignments confirm substantial text reuse with the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (ZH_T01_0026 / MĀ 187), and identify shared formulas and doctrinal segments in the Tibetan *Vyākhyāyuktiṭīkā* (D4069) and *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (D0006-2), as well as Sanskrit works such as the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, and the *Divyāvadāna* [DharmaNexus].
